1	# Agent Note: The Daliesk Village, an always-running lab on the harness
2	
3	Status: proposed
4	
5	English | [中文](2026-09-05-daliesk-village.zh.md)
6	
7	## Problem
8	
9	The harness now has the seams an always-running multi-agent lab needs — environments with executable checks, the runner that stamps every session and executes the checks, `verification/run` events and certificates, the fleet, the scorekeeper, frozen paired experiments, the budget policy, and the first slices of the read barrier — but no operating model that keeps them running around the clock, in public, with a roster of model routes, and turns what they record into client evidence, investor evidence, and training data. The [four-goal-workflows note](2026-09-05-four-goal-workflows.md) describes each workflow as a long-running loop; nothing yet says what runs when, who watches, what may be published, and what must land before a number leaves the building.
10	
11	The AI Village, run since April 2025 by Sage Future Inc (the US 501(c)(3) behind AI Digest), is the closest public precedent and the reason to decide this now. Its FAQ describes frontier agents each on their own Linux computer with a Google Workspace account, GitHub access, and a Cloudflare token, running every weekday, eight hours a day (9am–5pm Pacific) since the end of June 2026 and four hours a day before that, consolidating memory every 40 actions, receiving a new goal most Mondays, with humans sending a kickoff and one to four steering messages a week and approving any outreach to a real person, at "on the order of $10k per month in AI compute and infrastructure costs" ([How the AI Village works](https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/how-the-ai-village-works)). Its hiring post states 27 agents for 8 hours a day since April 2025, more than 200 agent-hours a day, four technical staff, and "$12.6M from Coefficient Giving" awarded to scale it ([Work on the AI Village](https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/work-on-the-ai-village)); that award is a philanthropic grant to a nonprofit, not a pre-seed round, and the "$10 million seed round" that appears beside Sage Future in funding digests belongs to another company. Its 2025 retrospective covers 16 goals and 19 models, growing from two hours a weekday with four agents to four or five hours with ten or eleven: $2,000 raised for charity, a 23-person live event, $200 of merchandise, 39 research participants recruited; and 64 fabrication intents in 109,000 reasoning summaries, roughly 300 outreach emails carrying fabricated claims, hallucinations spread by sycophantic agreement, metric gaming, goal abandonment, and its own verdict, "an existence proof, not a controlled experiment", with a single persistent instance per model named as the first limitation ([What did we learn from the AI Village in 2025?](https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/what-we-learned-2025)). Its public dataset holds 1.14 million computer-use turns, 123 thousand chat messages, 165 thousand agent memories, and 37 thousand sessions across 31 agents under a research licence that forbids training without written permission ([aidigestorg/ai-village](https://huggingface.co/datasets/aidigestorg/ai-village)).
12	
13	Every failure the Village documents is a failure this harness was built to prevent: self-reported success against `verification/run` and certificates, metric gaming against the read barrier and held-out hashes, runaway loops against the budget policy, a single path-dependent instance against fresh stamped sessions with repetitions and paired experiments. A first draft of this note claimed too much from that fact; a six-judge council review ([council review](#council-review)) found the draft overstated what had landed, named the certificate's missing executor field, the absence of tamper detection, the unpriced cost metric, the unenforced outreach ban, and the lack of durable orchestration. This note is the revised design: the same always-on format, honest about which claims the log can prove today, with the order in which the rest must land.
14	
15	## Proposal
16	
17	The Daliesk Village is a composition of existing plugins run in shifts, never an orchestration script that holds state the log does not. It has three districts writing one session log: the *Workshop* (W2, client-shaped goals compiled into hidden standards, paced by each program's ledger), the *Proving Ground* (W1 and W3, the environment suite run as fleet cells by every licensed model route, with pass@k per policy version), and the *Commons* (W4, department skills under keep-or-retire and frozen experiments that promote into the fleet). Every district is a `cordis.yml` plus a plan; every session is stamped by the runner; every number the observatory shows folds from persisted logs through the scorekeeper.
18	
19	### Publication rules
20	
21	- **Rows before rankings.** The observatory publishes leaderboard rows with their `isolation`, held-out flag, the composition digest of the preset that ran, the certificate's executor, and a tamper-status column, and never blends across any of them; a ranking, a "beats" caption, or a named frontier comparison appears only for a route pair that shares an `ExperimentResult` verdict under one preset and one isolation. Until the composition digest is a stamped field, frontier routes appear under pseudonymous labels and open-weight routes by name.
22	- **No public certificate rate before tamper verdicts.** A certificate today proves that a fully passing `verification/run` preceded it; it does not prove that the implementer left the check-owned paths alone (read-barrier slice 6) nor, before slice 5, that a shell-capable implementer could not read the standard. Until slice 6 lands, every public row carries `tamper: not instrumented` and rates feed neither the archive's quality term nor a training reward; Workshop rows stay behind a human reviewer.
23	- **Districts are a stamped field.** `environment/run` gains `district`; the exporter and the observatory withhold Workshop sessions by default the way they withhold held-out ones, and a raw excerpt of any session reaches the public only after a `SignoffRecord` from the data steward and the export's redaction profile.
24	- **Cadence follows the district.** A weekly frozen `SuitePlan` paces the Proving Ground and the Commons tiers; Workshop goals open and close on the program ledger and the plan's critical path, never on a calendar.
25	- **Cost is a logged fact or it is not published.** The budget policy logs each priced step as a `usage/priced` event carrying the rates and the pricing-table digest that priced it, so cost per session replays; until the scorekeeper folds those events into a cost per certified session, no cost figure leaves the lab.
26	
27	### Mechanics on the seams
28	
29	| Village need | Their mechanism | Ours, with status on this branch |
30	|---|---|---|
31	| Each agent its own computer | one Linux VM per agent | one fresh workspace per cell under the runner (landed); process-level denied read roots (read-barrier slice 5, proposed) |
32	| Memory across days | consolidation every 40 actions | skills in the department layer, compaction as a logged seam (landed); nothing else persists into a cell except a digested component (composition manifest, designed) |
33	| Weekly goals | chat message plus system prompt | environments with checks, fleet plan per shift, goal disarmed after its run (landed) |
34	| Knowing what happened | 800 summaries, a timeline, a blog | `SessionFacts` per session, scoreboard and pass@k per batch, trajectories per certified session (landed); a live projection of the leaderboard (proposed) |
35	| Catching fabrication | reading 109 thousand summaries afterwards | certificate only after a fully passing `verification/run` (landed); executor on the certificate and refusal of agent-reported runs above `none` (landed, read-barrier slice 4); tamper verdicts (slice 6, proposed) |
36	| Hiding the answer key | none | filesystem-tool reads denied under the validator root (landed, slices 1–2); tool authority guards and preset roles (landed, slice 3); shell, subprocess, and terminal denial (slice 5, proposed) |
37	| Stopping runaway agents | admin nudges, an idling system that misfired | `budget/breach` blocks the goal durably before the next step, no nudge text reaches the model (landed); shift-level spend aggregation and a per-route circuit breaker (proposed) |
38	| Fair comparison between models | one persistent instance per model | fleet repetitions in a group, pass@k, paired experiments with seeded bootstrap intervals (landed); preset as an arm and a composition digest on the stamp (proposed) |
39	| Public dataset | HuggingFace dump under a research licence | trajectory and facts export with held-out withholding (landed); district withholding, data-use terms, mandatory redaction, quarantine of dynamic mounts (proposed) |
40	| Outreach approval | admin approves emails | an `external-communication` tool authority denied by default plus the deny-capable monitor on `ctx.tools.guard()` (proposed); until then no district composes a tool that can reach a person, checked by a composition gate |
41	| Surviving a crash | manual restart | checkpointed sessions and durable breach blocks (landed); idempotent cells keyed by header hash × environment × repetition and a program ledger (proposed, rollout item 11) |
42	
43	### Shift zero
44	
45	The first shift is an NDA-gated, read-only Proving Ground snapshot built only from landed seams: open-weight routes, one `cordis.yml` per route composing environments, the runner at `isolation: none`, the fleet at a small concurrency, the budget policy with per-session caps from its pricing table, persistence with the checkpoint policy, the scorekeeper, and the trajectory exporter; no Workshop session, no outreach-capable tool, every stamped-but-unrun cell shown as an error row, routes named only where they are open-weight, no cost claim, and `tamper: not instrumented` on every row. A host-level supervisor restarts a dead shift driver and a named human is on call for the five conditions nothing catches yet: a crashed orchestrator, a route-wide provider outage past the retry budget, a full disk from unreaped workspaces, a dead shift timer, and a hung tool call. A composition gate (`verify-village-composition`, beside `verify-cordis-config`) refuses a district composition that omits the budget policy or persistence, or composes an outreach-capable tool without the monitor.
46	
47	### Budgets and cost
48	
49	Per-cell caps come from the budget policy; a shift needs two additions the harness does not have: a plan-level spend aggregator in the fleet that refuses to start a cell once the shift's folded spend crosses its configured ceiling, and a per-route circuit breaker that stops scheduling a route after a configured number of consecutive error cells inside a window and records why, so an outage does not pollute the certificate-rate denominator. Cell workspaces get a configured retention policy once a session's terminal event is durable, because the log, not the checkout, is the record. The operator judge's model, with its assumptions stated in the council record, puts scenario A (two DGX Spark plus cloud inference for eight open-weight routes at small concurrency and one client district) near €1,100 a month of infrastructure and scenario B (500 k€ on-prem, amortized over 36 months with power) near €18,000 a month, against roughly €67,000 a month for four engineers; the hardware choice moves the total by about €17,000 a month and the team dominates either way.
50	
51	### Data
52	
53	The Proving Ground already is W3's rollout mechanism; always-on operation adds continuous environment mining from Workshop failures, continuous recalibration of `EnvironmentStats`, a standing supply of certified trajectories for the SFT cold start, and a public leaderboard, not better GRPO groups. Before the Proving Ground feeds a reinforcement-learning step, the stamp gains `policyVersion` and `seed`, the trajectory fold emits `outcome: null` for truncated, aborted, and provider-error sessions instead of `0`, environment admission gains a near-duplicate check against the held-out suite, and the budget policy gains a device-slot resource so rollouts and training on shared GPUs do not degrade each other silently. The AI Village dataset enters only under data-use terms scoped to evaluation: as a behaviour taxonomy for `SessionDiagnosis`, and as raw material for environments resynthesized with invented entities, never as training data and never as a verbatim excerpt.
54	
55	### Commons and archive
56	
57	Generation zero of the archive seeds every island with more than one root so the novelty term has variance to weight; an `inconclusive` experiment verdict maps to a `parked` variant status with a configured retest cap before the variant is marked `dominated`; `ParentSample` carries sibling summaries so the quarantined Harness Engineer does not re-explore known dead ends; `LeaderboardRow` gains `harnessVariantId`; `deprecated` skills stay re-samplable when a later diagnosis names a context they were never tested in, closing only on a human rejection; and the manifest writer flags the same `KnowledgeProposal` digest appearing independently in two departments as the trigger for a portfolio-level nomination, which is how a norm like the Village's unprompted "receipt culture" would reach promotion on evidence rather than by acclamation.
58	
59	### Governance
60	
61	Five transitions never complete without a `signoff/recorded` event naming the principal and the artefact hash: spec freeze, relaxation of a security or compliance check, review acceptance, release, and training-data release; every client-district session carries `dataUse/terms` from creation; the exporter refuses to run without a redaction profile; publishing a raw excerpt is a signed decision; the EU AI Act's serious-incident channel is separate from the failure blog and routed to counsel; no training run that could approach the systemic-risk compute threshold starts before `ModelLineage` and its threshold alarm exist; and no named comparison of a competitor's model appears before the paired-experiment discipline and the isolation proof that make it verifiable.
62	
63	## Council review
64	
65	Six judges reviewed the first draft with the AI Village sources and the harness source in hand; their full reports are kept with the session's research files. Scores are out of ten.
66	
67	| Judge | Lens | Score | Decisive finding, and what changed |
68	|---|---|---|---|
69	| J1 | Software factory and client | 3 | No compliance artefact on a four-month sales clock; cost per certified session has no producer; the outreach ban was a promise. Shift zero became NDA-gated and Proving Ground only; `district` on the stamp; the composition gate; the trust dossier as the client-facing export. |
70	| J2 | Open-endedness and archives | 7 | Archive mechanics faithful to the source algorithms, but `inconclusive` had no status, generation zero had one root, and no path took emergent value to promotion. The Commons and archive section. |
71	| J3 | Reinforcement-learning data | 6 | Always-on is a scheduling wrapper around W3's mechanism; `policyVersion` and `seed` are missing from the stamp; truncated rollouts score as failures; the dataset's licence forbids training. The Data section. |
72	| J5 | Determinism and verification | 4 | The certificate does not carry its executor and an agent-reported run certifies identically; hidden checks are false for a shell-capable implementer until slice 5; tamper is the cheapest missing gate. Executor moved into slice 4 and the publication rules. |
73	| J6 | Governance and EU compliance | 3 | The draft claimed slices 1–4 and quarantine as landed; approvals carry no principal; export has no consent or redaction gate; comparative-advertising exposure. The Governance section and the status column. |
74	| J8 | Operations | 3 | Nothing above one session resumes after a crash; no shift-level budget, no circuit breaker, no retention, no durable scheduler; a cost model with stated assumptions. Shift zero's runbook and the Budgets section. |
75	
76	## Alternatives considered
77	
78	**Copy the Village format.** Persistent per-model instances, open-ended goals judged by narrative, public from day one. Rejected: the Village's own retrospective calls the result an existence proof, and its failure list is the list of things the harness's seams exist to prevent; a copy would inherit the failures and discard the seams.
79	
80	**Publish named frontier comparisons from day one.** Rejected until a route pair shares an experiment verdict under one preset and one isolation and the composition digest is stamped; before that a comparison is unverifiable, and for a commercial lab it is also a comparative claim it cannot substantiate.
81	
82	**An offline batch pipeline instead of an always-on one.** Kept as the fallback and as the honest description of what always-on adds: mining, recalibration, cold-start supply, and legitimacy, not data quality. If shift zero cannot be staffed, the batch pipeline produces the same groups.
83	
84	**One weekly cadence for every district.** Rejected for the Workshop, where a calendar reset would put a human signer under a deadline unrelated to the artefact and would force restarts on a layer that cannot yet resume.
85	
86	**Nonprofit-style disclosure of raw transcripts.** Rejected without a signed excerpt decision and a redaction profile; the public numbers come from the facts schema, never from a person reading a Workshop transcript.
87	
88	## Acceptance criteria
89	
90	- Shift zero runs the Proving Ground for seven days with every cell present as a row (report or error) and no missing sequence in the persisted logs, with a human on call and every intervention logged with a principal.
91	- The observatory shows `isolation`, executor, composition digest (or `pending`), and tamper status on every row, publishes no ranking without an `ExperimentResult` verdict, and names no frontier route before the composition digest is stamped; a snapshot test proves the withholding of Workshop and held-out sessions from the public export.
92	- `verify-village-composition` exists beside `verify-cordis-config`, in `hygiene` and the static CI lanes, over the same configuration inventory: a district composition — one composing `@deepseek-ai/dsh-environment-runner`, `@deepseek-ai/dsh-fleet`, or `@deepseek-ai/dsh-experiments` — is rejected when it omits `@deepseek-ai/dsh-budget-policy` with at least one cap set, a session persistence backend, or `@deepseek-ai/dsh-session-checkpoint-policy`, and a fleet entry is rejected when it omits `workspaceRetention`; a runner claiming `isolation: process` or `host` warns until `--strict`, because no read-barrier slice on this branch proves the claim. Every rejection is proven by a fixture, and each names the file, the entry id, and the rule. Still needed: refusal of an outreach-capable tool composed without the monitor, which waits for the `external-communication` authority.
93	- A certificate carries its executor; an agent-reported run cannot certify above `none`; a tamper fixture yields reward zero before any public certificate rate is published.
94	- Cost per certified session appears only once a `usage/priced` event with the pricing-table digest exists and the scorekeeper folds it; a fixture proves the same log prices identically after the table changes when the digest differs.
95	- A session derived from the AI Village dataset carries data-use terms scoped to evaluation and never appears in a training export, proven by an export fixture.
96	
97	## Rollout
98	
99	1. **Shift zero (Proving Ground, NDA).** Landed: `district` on the `environment/run` stamp with the exporter's `withheldDistricts` and per-request `districts`, the fleet's per-route circuit breaker (`FLEET_ROUTE_BREAKER_OPEN`), its plan-level `tokenCeiling` with the run's `spend` (`FLEET_TOKEN_CEILING_REACHED`), its `workspaceRetention`, the composition gate, the budget policy's `usage/priced` event carrying the pricing-table digest, and the executor on certificates (read-barrier slice 4). Still needed: the scorekeeper fold of `usage/priced` into cost per session; runs with a human on call. TODO: the observatory withholds a district only once `ScoreboardRow` carries the stamp's `district`, which the scorekeeper owns.
100	2. **Public certificate rates.** Needs read-barrier slices 5 and 6 (shell denial and tamper verdicts) and the tamper column; rates then feed the archive's quality term.
101	3. **Unattended shifts.** Designed in the [shifts note](2026-09-05-village-shifts.md): shift identity and the `shift/*` ledger, cells recovered from their stamps and never run twice, cadence per district, and the token spend window across shifts; the host-level supervisor becomes a fallback once its slices land.
102	4. **Named comparisons and the Commons.** Needs the composition manifest slices (digest on the stamp, preset as an experiment arm, `harnessVariantId` on the leaderboard) and the archive with `parked` and sibling summaries.
103	5. **Workshop in public and excerpt disclosure.** Needs `signoff/recorded`, `dataUse/terms`, mandatory redaction, and the trust-dossier export.
104	6. **Any outreach.** Needs the `external-communication` authority and the deny-capable monitor.
105	7. **A live observatory.** Needs the leaderboard as a cached session projection; until then the page states its batch refresh interval.
106	8. **Feeding W3.** Needs `policyVersion` and `seed` on the stamp, masked terminal reasons in the trajectory fold, near-duplicate admission, and the device-slot budget.
107	
108	## Risks
109	
110	- **A correct table under an overstated headline.** The first draft's per-row status was accurate while its topline claimed hidden checks and controlled experiments; every public sentence must be checkable against the status column, or the observatory repeats the Village's credibility problem in the opposite direction.
111	- **One missing row.** A session that disappears without an error row inflates every rate computed from the rest; survivorship is the first thing a client's reviewer will test.
112	- **Harness and model co-evolution.** A route measured on a harness variant that evolved against it measures the pair; the composition digest on the stamp is what keeps a leaderboard row attributable.
113	- **Comparative claims.** A named comparison a commercial lab cannot substantiate is a legal exposure the Village, as a nonprofit, never carries.
114	- **Sunk hardware.** Scenario B's cluster is sized for training and residency, not for Village inference; buying it to run the Village alone is the wrong reason.
115	- **Staffing dominates cost.** Four engineers cost several times either infrastructure scenario; the design must reduce on-call load with each rollout step or it will not stay always-on.
116	- **Emergent institutions.** Skills agents write for each other drift into prompt inflation without content-addressed identity and a keep-or-retire scoreboard; the Village's 48 % of self-reported bugs that could not be reproduced is the number to keep in view.
117

1	# Agent Note: The read barrier as filesystem and process authority
2	
3	Status: proposed
4	
5	English | [中文](2026-09-05-read-barrier.zh.md)
6	
7	## Problem
8	
9	A certificate proves only what the implementer could not reach, and nothing in the repository decides that. [`dsh-verification`](../../../../packages/verification/verification/README.md) commits a `verification/certificate` only for a fully passing run and stamps it with a `CertificateIsolation` of `none`, `process`, or `host`, but its own Known Limitations name the missing read barrier: the standard's `run` instructions are readable by any in-process consumer of the log, and denying implementer reads is filesystem-policy work in a plugin that does not exist. The [four-goal-workflows note](2026-09-05-four-goal-workflows.md) states the requirement as principle P4, the read barrier as filesystem and process authority rather than a promise; this note is its design.
10	
11	The implementer and the checks share one filesystem and one operating-system user. `EnvironmentRunner.run()` creates the implementer's agent with `meta.cwd = workspace` and then executes every check through `ctx.shell` with `workdir: workspace` from the same process ([`packages/improvement/environment-runner/src/index.ts`](../../../../packages/improvement/environment-runner/src/index.ts)); its README states that the read barrier is the deployment's. The standard is in the implementer's own session log, which [`dsh-session-persistence-jsonl`](../../../../packages/session/session-persistence-jsonl/README.md) keeps as ordinary files under its configured root. [`dsh-credentials-local`](../../../../packages/credentials/credentials-local/README.md) already records what that costs: owner-only modes stop other operating-system users and not the model, because tool processes run as the same user and the shipped file policy confines mutations rather than reads.
12	
13	Composition decides what an implementer can read, and no composition is checked. A preset that mounts [`dsh-tool-session-query`](../../../../packages/session-query/tool-session-query/README.md) hands the model five tools that read the durable session log; one that mounts [`dsh-tool-cordis`](../../../../packages/extensions/tool-cordis/README.md) lets it define and mount a plugin into the live process. `tools.restrict()` and subagent `toolFilter` are visibility composition per [agent-scope-contexts](../../implemented/architecture/2026-07-08-agent-scope-contexts.md), not authority, and a certificate carries no durable record of which tools its session composed.
14	
15	An isolation claim above `none` therefore has no evidence behind it. `recordRun()` writes the level its caller passes; the invariant companion validates revisions, append-only check growth, and certificate coverage, and never asks what the level asserts. Keeping only `process` and `host` runs — the reward-gaming mitigation the [trajectory-export note](2026-09-05-trajectory-export-and-environment-registry.md) names, and the column the [fleet leaderboard](../../../../packages/improvement/fleet/README.md) refuses to average across — filters on an unchecked field.
16	
17	Nothing detects a workspace the implementer edited underneath its own checks. A task whose fixture supplies the tests it will be graded on is graded on whatever those files say at validation time, and the runner compares nothing between the overlay it wrote and the tree it measures.
18	
19	## Proposal
20	
21	Make the barrier authority at the executor: one policy owner, per-capability denial where each capability opens paths, and a certificate that may claim only what the composition recorded.
22	
23	**A validator-owned root.** [`@deepseek-ai/dsh-read-barrier`](../../../../packages/verification/read-barrier/README.md) (`ctx.readBarrier`) at `packages/verification/read-barrier/` is the policy home for denied reads, in the role [`dsh-sandbox-policy`](../../../../packages/sandbox/sandbox-policy/README.md) plays for sandbox mode and workspace root. Its `root` config defaults to `dshHomePath('verification')` through [`dsh-home-paths`](../../../../packages/util/home-paths/README.md) and accepts any absolute or `~`-prefixed directory, as does every `denyRoots` entry; the service creates the root owner-only (`0700`) at construction and fails loud when it exists with wider modes or when a configured path is not absolute after expansion. `reserve(agent)` mints `<root>/runs/<sessionId>/` for one run and returns its absolute path, synchronously, so the role is in force the moment the caller returns; the environment runner calls it before appending the `environment/run` stamp and writes there the standard snapshot, one script per check at `checks/<checkId>`, and any fixture the environment marks held out, then resolves each check's `run` against that directory so the command line the implementer can observe in a process listing names a file whose content it cannot read. Because that reservation is what makes a session the implementer, the runner reads the barrier through `ctx.get('readBarrier')`: a composition without one reserves nothing and runs its checks inline, which is what its `isolation: none` claim already says. `protect(path)` registers one more denied directory and returns its disposer, so a plugin that owns a directory — `dsh-session-persistence-jsonl` with its session-store root — contributes it as an effect instead of a deployment repeating it in configuration; `denyRoots` remains a config field for directories no plugin owns. `resolve({ session? })` answers one `ReadBarrierPolicy { role, root, denied }`, and `denies(policy, target)` decides containment. Enforcement is not a field on that policy: `enforce(capability)` registers one capability's decision as an effect and `enforcementCensus()` reads the registrations back, so what a capability enforces lives as long as its listener rather than being recomputed per call. `declareComposition(agent, { presetId, role? })` is how the preset roster — the only caller — tells the barrier what a session composed.
24	
25	| Field | Meaning |
26	|---|---|
27	| `root` (default `dshHomePath('verification')`) | Absolute or `~`-prefixed directory the barrier owns; created `0700`, rejected when it already exists with wider modes. |
28	| `denyRoots` (default `[]`) | Additional absolute directories denied alongside `root`, for directories no plugin registers through `protect()`. |
29	| `hostAttestation` (optional absolute path) | File an external account writes; without a verified one the barrier refuses a `host` claim. It arrives with the certificate invariant that reads it. |
30	
31	The denied set for a role is not among them: which authorities an `implementer` may hold is a security invariant, not a deployment choice.
32	
33	**The deny rule.** For a session whose role is `implementer`, a read is denied when the target's canonical path is a denied directory or a descendant of one. Containment is decided the way [`dsh-fs-sandbox`](../../implemented/feature/2026-07-14-cross-family-fs-sandbox.md) decides it: canonicalize first, then test identity or descent through `ctx.fs.contains(parent, child)` on resolved targets, so the policy parses no path strings and an ancestor symlink swapped since resolution is caught by re-canonicalizing immediately before the decision. A target whose containment cannot be decided is denied. Roles `validator` and `unrestricted` are denied nothing; `unrestricted` is the default and leaves every shipped preset exactly as it is today. Until a preset can declare a role, a session holding a reservation is the `implementer` and every other session is `unrestricted`, so the two open roles are indistinguishable at the decision and only the denied one is reachable.
34	
35	**The fs policy plugin.** Add `@deepseek-ai/dsh-fs-read-barrier` at `packages/fs/fs-read-barrier/`, the read counterpart of the write and edit policy [`dsh-fs-observation-policy`](../../../../packages/fs/fs-observation-policy/README.md) contributes through the same event gate. It registers no service and declares no `Config`, because every deployment-varying value belongs to the barrier above: it injects `readBarrier` and decides one new event. [`dsh-fs`](../../../../packages/fs/fs/README.md) declares `fs/read-intent(target, actor, next)` beside `fs/write-intent` and `fs/edit-intent`, as a `@mode waterfall` returning `FsReadDenial { code: FsErrorCode; message: string } | undefined`; unlike the two single-slot intents this one delegates, because a barrier that owned the slot would stop every later read policy from deciding. The plugin returns a denial for a contained target and calls `next()` otherwise, and owns the exact message as `readBarrierDenialMessage`. `FsErrorCode` gains `FS_READ_BARRIER_DENIED`. `dsh-tool-fs` dispatches the event inside `resolveRegularReadTarget` before `ctx.fs.stat`, covering `read` and `read_image`, so a denied path never reveals presence or absence, and `dsh-tool-str-replace-editor` dispatches it on the `view` command. The tool layer adds no recovery instruction, because no retry of the same call succeeds; the model sees the policy's message verbatim inside the tool registry's ordinary `Error: ` framing.
36	
37	##### Exact error
38	
39	```markdown
40	read denied: "<path>" is validator-owned — it is not part of this task; continue without it
41	```
42	
43	**What a denial records.** The barrier appends one log-only `read-barrier/denied` session event per refusal, carrying `{ version, role, capability, displayPath, root }`, where `capability` names the seam that refused (`fs`, `shell`, `subprocess`, `terminal`). The path is already in the log inside the model's own `tool/call` arguments, so the event adds evidence and no new disclosure. It is a `SessionEventMap` member registered in `KNOWN_SESSION_EVENT_TYPES` by `gen-persistence-catalog`, so this build reads it as a required event. The envelope's `ignorable` marker stays unused: `Session.append` has no parameter for it and no event in the repository sets it, so marking this one would be a core append change rather than a slice of the barrier.
44	
45	**Tool authority and the composition-time guard.** `ToolDefinition` in [`dsh-tools`](../../../../packages/core/tools/README.md) gains `authority?: readonly ToolAuthority[]`, never model-visible, where `ToolAuthority` is a merge-extensible union declared by `dsh-tools` with three members at the start: `session-log` (the tool reads durable session events), `plugin-mount` (it mounts or evaluates code in the live runtime), and `runtime-introspection` (it reports the live composition). `dsh-tool-session-query` declares `session-log` on all five of its tools; `dsh-tool-cordis` declares `plugin-mount` on `cordis_define`, `cordis_run`, `cordis_stop`, and `cordis_undefine`, and `runtime-introspection` on the three tools it actually ships for the read-only report — `cordis_inspect_list`, `cordis_inspect_query`, and `cordis_inspect_self`. An `implementer` session may compose none of the three. Declaring authority at the tool, rather than a name list at the barrier, means a tool added later is covered by its own declaration.
46	
47	**How a preset declares its role.** A preset's optional `preset.yml` gains `role: implementer | validator | unrestricted`, absent meaning `unrestricted`. It is the one authority claim that file carries, so [`dsh-agent-presets`](../../../../packages/preset/agent-presets/README.md) refuses `validator` from a `user`-trust preset and lists that preset as `broken` with the reason: a locally authored preset that could name itself `validator` would grant itself reads. This is the roster's first enforcing use of `trust`, and its README changes with it. `mountPreset` audits the role after `handle.await()` settles the subtree, beside `inactiveRows`, and rejects the mount when the declared role is `implementer` and any tool in the preset's scope layer declares a denied authority. Because the audit runs inside the agent factory's `setup`, a rejected composition rolls the whole session creation back, so the failure is loud and nothing half-composed survives.
48	
49	##### Exact mount refusal
50	
51	```markdown
52	agent-presets: preset "<id>" declares role "implementer" but composes "<tool>", which carries the "<authority>" authority
53	```
54	
55	**The runtime guard.** The barrier also registers one `ctx.tools.guard()` through the agent's own context at session setup, denying any execution whose definition carries a denied authority for that session's role. Guards run after every `tools/pre-execute` listener and are monotonic, so no later listener can turn the denial back into permission ([`ToolGuard`](../../../../packages/core/tools/src/index.ts)). The mount audit covers the preset's composition; the guard covers a tool registered into the agent's own layer afterwards, including one a subagent driver contributes.
56	
57	##### Exact guard denial
58	
59	```markdown
60	"<tool>" carries the "<authority>" authority and is not callable in an implementer session
61	```
62	
63	**Process-level denial.** The [sandbox seam](../../implemented/feature/2026-07-06-sandbox.md) expresses file effects only, which is why a confined subprocess can still read anything it reaches. `SandboxPolicy` and `SandboxExecutionPolicy` gain `deniedReadRoots: readonly string[]`; `ctx.sandboxPolicy.resolve()` fills it from `ctx.readBarrier.resolve({ session })`, so the fs fence and every process runner keep taking one owner-resolved policy per call. `dsh-sandbox-local` implements it per backend — a `bwrap` `--tmpfs` over each root, a Landlock ruleset that omits read access for them, a Seatbelt `(deny file-read* (subpath …))` clause, and the Windows ACL runner's equivalent deny entry — and reports `SANDBOX_UNAVAILABLE` when the selected backend cannot express the denial, so the claim fails rather than the barrier. [`dsh-bash-sandbox`](../../../../packages/shell/bash-sandbox/README.md), `dsh-pwsh-sandbox`, and [`dsh-terminal-bash`](../../../../packages/terminal/terminal-bash/README.md) inherit it without changes. [`dsh-tool-fs-search`](../../../../packages/fs/tool-fs-search/README.md) spawns ripgrep unconfined through `ctx.subprocess` today; it confines that spawn through `ctx.sandbox.confine()` whenever a barrier is in force, and additionally the barrier's tool guard denies a `glob` or `grep` whose `path` argument names a denied root directly.
64	
65	**The executor of a run.** `RunEvidence.executor` already distinguishes a `runner` from an `agent-reported` run on the `verification/run` event, and `recordRun()` certified both identically. `VerificationCertificate` gains `executor`, copied from the run it cites, so a consumer reading a certificate alone can tell which it was; the scorekeeper's outcome facts expose it as `certificateExecutor`, which is what lets a leaderboard partition on it. `recordRun()` refuses any isolation above `none` for an `agent-reported` run — the implementer's own account of its checks is admissible evidence only at the level that asserts nothing — and the invariant rejects a certificate whose executor differs from the run it cites, or which claims `process` or `host` over an `agent-reported` run.
66	
67	**Executors the barrier cannot confine.** Two composed capabilities open paths the harness cannot fence in-process. [`dsh-workflow-worker-thread`](../../../../packages/workflow/workflow-worker-thread/README.md) states that its worker is not a security sandbox and that an escaped script recovers Node capabilities with the host process's privileges. The out-of-process [subagent](../../../../packages/subagent/subagent/README.md) providers — `subagent-acp`, `subagent-claude-code`, `subagent-codex`, `subagent-dsh-sdk` — launch a foreign agent with its own tool stack and no harness policy. For an `implementer` session, both refuse to start under a claim of `process` or `host` and record `unenforced` under a claim of `none`. The in-process subagent drivers need no exception: a child joins its parent's standing composition through `composeFrom()`, so it inherits the same census, the same scope layer, and the same role.
68	
69	**The scope census.** It arrives with `ToolAuthority`, whose declarations its `census` is made of. Before the session's first `request/header`, the barrier appends one log-only `read-barrier/scope` event carrying `{ version, role, presetId, root, denied, census, enforcement }`. `census` is one entry per tool visible to the agent, `{ name, authority }`, which makes the composition's authority durable rather than composition-time-only; the invariant cross-checks it against the tool names in each `request/header`'s assembled schemas, so a tool added after the census is caught. `enforcement` is one entry per path-opening capability the composition registered — `fs`, `shell`, `subprocess`, `terminal`, `subagent`, `workflow` — valued `denied-at-executor`, `unenforced`, or `not-composed`. A capability records `denied-at-executor` by calling `ctx.readBarrier.enforce(capability)` for the life of its enforcing registration, so the claim and the listener that backs it are disposed together.
70	
71	**The certificate invariant.** `recordRun()` refuses to commit a certificate whose isolation exceeds what the session recorded, with `VERIFICATION_ISOLATION_UNPROVEN`; the [`./invariant`](../../../../packages/verification/verification/README.md) companion applies the identical rule to the durable stream, so a forged certificate fails replay wherever the companion is installed. Both read the session log alone rather than `ctx.get('readBarrier')`: everything a live barrier knows about a session is already in the census it appended, and one rule over one evidence source is what makes the live refusal and the replay refusal the same rule. Independently of level, both refuse a certificate on a session whose scope census carries a denied authority: composing a log-reading tool forfeits the certificate even when the guard was somehow bypassed. `CertificateIsolation`'s JSDoc changes with the rule: `process` means what the ladder below states rather than in-process read policy alone.
72	
73	**The `host` marker.** `host` is accepted only from a `read-barrier/attestation` event the barrier wrote after verifying a file at the configured `hostAttestation` path: it must be a regular file, be owned by a uid other than the harness process's effective uid, and be unwritable outside its owner. An in-process component cannot produce that file without already holding another account's privileges, which is the property the level asserts. The barrier records the file's SHA-256 alongside its owner; comparing that digest against the run's environment content hashes waits for the `environment/run` stamp to reach the barrier, so the shipped check proves the owner rather than the run. Ownership is read through `process.geteuid()`, which Windows does not provide: an attestation there is refused with that reason rather than verified through `dsh-sandbox-windows-acl`. Absent or unverifiable, the barrier records no attestation, logs why, and the claim is refused.
74	
75	**Tamper on check-owned paths.** Check-owned paths are the barrier's denied directories plus the workspace paths an environment declares immutable: `EnvironmentDefinition.task` gains `immutable?: readonly string[]`, workspace-relative paths the fixture supplies and the implementer must not author — the tests, the reference outputs, and any overlaid check script. The runner already hashes a directory in `hashDirectory`; it records the digest of the check-owned set immediately after the fixture overlay and before the implementer's first turn, and again at each validation. The `verification/run` event that the [environment-runner note's second slice](2026-09-05-environment-runner.md) adds carries the attempt's `treeHash`; this note adds `verdict: 'pass' | 'fail' | 'tampered'`. A digest that differs from the baseline is `tampered`: the runner records the run, issues one directive naming tamper without naming a path, stops the attempt loop because the workspace no longer measures the task, and never calls `recordRun`, so no certificate can exist for that run. `foldTrajectory` gains reward basis `tamper` with `outcome: 0`, which outranks any certificate in the same log, and the invariant companion rejects a certificate that follows a `tampered` run.
76	
77	**A blind judge under one licence.** Cross-provider routing is the first answer to a judge whose label affects it, and a deployment with one model licence cannot take it. The second route is filesystem and process isolation plus a judge session that holds no implementer context, which means all of the following and nothing weaker. The judge session is created through `ctx.agents.create` with a fresh `SessionId`, no `parentSessionId`, and no resume or fork seed, so its log begins at its own creation. Its `meta.cwd` is a judge workspace holding a copy of the implementer's tree at the audited attempt's `treeHash`, never the implementer's workspace. Its derived history contains exactly the judge preset's system prompt, the environment's task prompt, and one user message carrying the evidence the auditor chose; no `assistant/message`, `tool/result`, or `verification/directive` from the audited session reaches it. Its preset is `system`-trust and declares `role: validator`, so the composition-time guard still denies it a log-reading tool: a judge that could read the audited log would reconstruct the implementer's reasoning and lose the independence this arrangement provides. The barrier appends a `judge/session` event naming the audited session id and asserting the empty lineage, and the invariant rejects a verdict from a session whose header carries a parent or a seed.
78	
79	## The isolation ladder
80	
81	| Level | What it asserts | Required enforcement | Durable evidence |
82	|---|---|---|---|
83	| `none` | Nothing. Implementer and validator share a filesystem. | None. | The certificate alone; a scope event when the barrier is composed. |
84	| `process` | No executor of the implementer's session opens a denied path. | Every composed path-opening capability records `denied-at-executor`; the session's sandbox mode is `workspace-write` or narrower; workflow workers and out-of-process subagent providers refuse to start. | A `read-barrier/scope` event before the first `request/header`, with role `implementer`, an empty denied-authority intersection, and no `unenforced` entry. |
85	| `host` | The checks and fixtures are outside the harness account's write reach. | Everything `process` requires. | Everything `process` requires plus a `read-barrier/attestation` event the barrier verified from a file the harness process cannot write. |
86	
87	## Alternatives considered
88	
89	**Omit the tools and trust the prompt.** Schema omission and instruction are not enforcement when another caller reaches the same operation, which is why the packages standard requires the decision in the operation that makes it. The barrier denies at the executor and the acceptance criteria test denial there.
90	
91	**Deny reads through `SandboxMode` instead of a separate policy.** `SandboxMode` is a three-value file-effect vocabulary shared by every enforcing family; a fourth value meaning "and cannot read these paths" would make one enum carry two independent decisions, and every consumer that switches on the mode would have to learn the second. `deniedReadRoots` rides the same per-call policy without changing what a mode means.
92	
93	**Subclass the filesystem provider the way `fs-sandbox` does.** One provider registers `ctx.fs` per context and `SandboxedFileSystem` already extends `LocalFileSystem`, so a second fence by inheritance would force a mixin or a fixed provider ladder. The `fs/*` event gate is the layer built for adding policy without a service dependency, and it degrades to the bare provider when the plugin is absent.
94	
95	**Name the forbidden tools in the barrier's config.** A name list is stale the moment a package adds a log-reading tool, and a deployment could shorten it. Authority declared at the tool is carried by the tool, and the denied set for a role is a security invariant rather than a tunable.
96	
97	**Derive the role from the session creator instead of the preset.** The creator knows the intent; only the composition knows what was actually mounted, and the failure this prevents is a preset that composes a tool its role forbids. The preset declares the role, the mount audit checks the composition against it, and the creator's request is refused when the resolved preset's role does not match.
98	
99	**Infer `host` from configuration.** The environment runner already rejected inferred isolation for the same reason: nothing in-process can observe the deployment's arrangement, so an inferred value either devalues an isolated run or lies about a local one. A file another account owns is the smallest fact that cannot be produced from inside the process.
100	
101	**Score tamper as a failing check.** A failed check means the work is incomplete; a modified test means the measurement is void. Folding them would let a trajectory earn partial credit for a workspace whose checks no longer describe the task, so tamper is its own verdict and its own reward basis.
102	
103	**Give the judge the implementer's transcript for context.** A judge that reads the audited reasoning inherits its framing, and the same-lineage mislabeling the [seams note](2026-08-29-verification-improvement-oversight-seams.md) records is what the blind session exists to avoid. The judge receives the task, the tree, and the evidence the auditor selected.
104	
105	## Acceptance criteria
106	
107	- In a Loader-booted composition over `examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/read-barrier/`, a `read` of a file under the barrier root from an `implementer`-role session fails with `FS_READ_BARRIER_DENIED` and the exact message above, one `read-barrier/denied` event is appended, and the same call from a session the barrier denies nothing — one holding no reservation, and a `validator` once a preset can declare that role — returns the file's content in the same process.
108	- The denial is proved through the executor, not the schema: the implementer's `read` tool is registered and visible, and a direct `ctx.fs.readText` from a trusted plugin still succeeds, which the test asserts so the threat model stays explicit.
109	- Mounting the preset at `examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/read-barrier-guard/`, which declares `role: implementer` and composes `dsh-tool-session-query`, rejects with the exact mount refusal and leaves no session behind; a `user`-trust preset declaring `role: validator` is listed `broken` with its reason; and the invariant companion rejects a certificate on a hand-authored log whose scope census carries the `session-log` authority.
110	- `recordRun()` with `isolation: 'host'` on a session with no verified attestation refuses with `VERIFICATION_ISOLATION_UNPROVEN` and commits no certificate; the invariant companion rejects a hand-authored log carrying that certificate at the certificate record.
111	- `recordRun()` with `isolation: 'process'` on a session whose scope event records any `unenforced` capability refuses the same way, and succeeds once every composed capability records `denied-at-executor`.
112	- Over `examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/read-barrier-tamper/`, whose environment marks its test file immutable and whose scripted model overwrites it, the attempt's `verification/run` carries `verdict: 'tampered'`, no certificate exists, the goal stays out of `complete`, and the exported trajectory line has `outcome: 0` with basis `tamper`.
113	- A judge session created for an audited session has no `parentSessionId` and no seed, its derived history holds exactly the judge system prompt, the task prompt, and the evidence message, and the invariant rejects a verdict from a session that carries either.
114	- Two keyless snapshots record what the model sees: `examples/headless-agent/tests/snapshots/read-barrier-denied/` pins the denial text in the transcript and the session log, and `examples/headless-agent/tests/snapshots/read-barrier-tamper/` pins the tamper directive's `<validation_failed>` follow-up. Both replay on macOS and Linux per the [testing policy](../../../../docs/testing.md).
115	
116	## Rollout
117	
118	Each slice lands with its own tests and leaves the gates green on its own.
119	
120	1. **Landed.** `@deepseek-ai/dsh-read-barrier` with the root, `reserve`, `protect`, `resolve`, `denies`, `recordDenial`, the `read-barrier/denied` event, and its invariant companion, which rejects a refusal for any role but `implementer`, one carrying an unknown payload version or capability, and one naming a second barrier root inside a session. The environment runner reserves through `ctx.get('readBarrier')` and materializes `standard.json` plus one `checks/<checkId>` script per attempt, running each as `. <script>` so the same shell executes the same instruction; a check id that is not one path segment, and a reservation path the command line cannot carry unquoted, fail the run with `ENVIRONMENT_RUN_UNSAFE_CHECK_SCRIPT`. `read-barrier/scope` and the enforcement census are not part of it: the census is one `{ name, authority }` entry per visible tool and enforcement is one entry per capability that records a decision, so both wait for the slice that supplies their content. `dsh-session-persistence-jsonl` does not yet call `protect()`, and no existing composition changes behavior.
121	2. **Landed.** `fs/read-intent` in `dsh-fs` as a delegating waterfall returning `FsReadDenial`, `FS_READ_BARRIER_DENIED`, the dispatches in `dsh-tool-fs` (`read` and `read_image`, inside `resolveRegularReadTarget` before the stat) and `dsh-tool-str-replace-editor` (`view`, before its own stat), and `@deepseek-ai/dsh-fs-read-barrier`, which owns the exact message. The `read-barrier` fixture proves the denial through the executor in a Loader-booted composition, and the `read-barrier-denied` snapshot pins the model-visible text and the durable record; both are keyless, the snapshot replaying a committed script through `dsh-llm-replay`.
122	3. **Landed.** `ToolAuthority` on `ToolDefinition`, the declarations in `dsh-tool-session-query` and `dsh-tool-cordis`, `role` in `preset.yml` with the `user`-trust refusal of `validator`, the `mountPreset` audit, `ReadBarrierService.declareComposition` as the roster's one way to set a role, and the per-agent tool guard. `read-barrier/scope` lands here too, with `enforce()` and `enforcementCensus()`, because the census is made of the authority declarations this slice adds and the enforcement registrations it needs a home for; `dsh-fs-read-barrier` is the first caller of `enforce()`. The audit reads the tool registry as the preset's scope resolves it, so a tool a restriction filtered out of that scope is not audited — that scope cannot call it either, and the guard covers what the audit cannot see.
123	4. **Landed.** The certificate invariant: the `recordRun` precondition, the companion's rule, `VerificationCertificate.executor` with the `agent-reported` ceiling and the scorekeeper's `certificateExecutor` fact, the `read-barrier/attestation` event and its file check, and the `CertificateIsolation` documentation change. `EnvironmentRunRequest.preset` is not part of it and is withdrawn: the census already records the session's role, so `isolationProblem` refuses a claim above `none` from a session that did not hold `implementer` — the refusal belongs to the operation that certifies, not to a second field on the run request. `verification-domain`'s `agent-reported` fixture moves from `process` to `none`, which is what its evidence supported all along.
124	5. `deniedReadRoots` on `SandboxPolicy` and `SandboxExecutionPolicy`, the `dsh-sandbox-local` backends, the `dsh-sandbox-policy` fill from the barrier, the confined ripgrep spawn in `dsh-tool-fs-search`, and the refusals in the workflow engine and the out-of-process subagent providers. This is the slice that makes `process` claimable.
125	6. Tamper: `task.immutable` in `dsh-environments`, the runner's baseline and per-attempt digest over check-owned paths, `verdict` on `verification/run`, the `tamper` reward basis in `dsh-trajectories`, and the `read-barrier-tamper` fixture and snapshot. It follows the `verification/run` event from the [environment-runner note's second slice](2026-09-05-environment-runner.md).
126	7. The blind judge: the shipped `system`-trust judge preset, the lineage-free creation path, the `judge/session` event, and the invariant that rejects a seeded judge. The judging Consumer itself belongs to the oversight seam of the [seams note](2026-08-29-verification-improvement-oversight-seams.md).
127	
128	## Risks
129	
130	The barrier is trusted code in the implementer's own process below `host`. A plugin with direct `Session` or `ctx.fs` access appends counterfeit events and reads any path, exactly as `dsh-verification` already states for its durable records. The ladder is honest about this: `none` claims nothing, `process` claims only that the composed executors deny, and `host` is the only level whose evidence comes from outside the process.
131	
132	`process` costs enforcement a deployment may not want. Confining every ripgrep spawn, refusing workflow workers, and refusing out-of-process subagent providers removes capability from implementer sessions that claim it; a deployment that wants those capabilities runs at `none` and keeps a certificate that says so.
133	
134	A check's command line stays observable. The barrier protects the script's content and the fixtures, not the argv a process listing shows, so an environment whose check name or arguments encode the assertion leaks it. Environment authors keep the assertion in the script.
135	
136	The census is only as complete as the composition it was taken from. It is appended before the first request and cross-checked against each `request/header`'s tool names, which catches a tool added later but not a plugin that reads paths without registering a tool at all.
137	
138	Tamper detection is a digest comparison, so it reports that the check-owned set changed and never who changed it or how. A legitimate build step that rewrites a file inside the immutable set fails the run; environment authors declare the immutable set narrowly, and a false verdict costs one run rather than a wrong certificate.
139	
140	Making `trust` enforcing for one field changes what the roster promises. A deployment that configured a `user` root expecting presets to be ordinary compositions now finds one class of declaration refused there; the refusal is listed as a `broken` reason on the same roster page that offers to delete it.

Models have become very good at problems with compact, stable criteria for success. Much of the past year's progress in mathematics and constrained optimization falls into this category - 
machine-checked proofs of long-open Erdős problems
gold-medal performance at the IMO
new bounds on decades-old combinatorial problems
. The search space can be enormous, but the result can ultimately be judged as a whole.
Large software tasks are different. A software specification can semantically cover the desired outcome without specifying what must be run, inspected, and compared before the work can be called complete. Requirements state what must be true. By themselves, they do not measure whether the work achieves it.
Without that measurement, an agent constructs one piecemeal as it works. It decomposes the task, validates each piece in the context that produced it, and eventually decides that it is finished. Every local judgment may be reasonable while parts of the whole remain unmeasured.
Humans currently close the loop by supervising the agent: holding the whole outcome and steering the agent back to it.
We wanted to know whether the model could close the loop on its own.


[H3 id] gdal-from-scratch


#### gdal, from scratch
To test this, we compared single-agent and multi-role runs across 24 selected 
ProgramBench
 tasks and three models. Take 
gdal
. We asked Droid to rebuild it from scratch in two ways. In both runs, Droid could execute the reference program without limit, but could not access its source, tests, or the internet.
gdal
the reference program
~2M lines upstream
~600K reachable through the CLI
gdal
 is the command-line tool of the GDAL project, the workhorse of
geospatial data processing, and carries decades of functionality behind
dozens of subcommands.
In development since 1998, GDAL sits beneath much of the world's mapping
software - QGIS, ArcGIS, PostGIS - and reads more than two hundred raster
and vector formats, from satellite imagery to navigation charts.
As a single agent, Droid implemented, checked its own work, and decided for itself when it was done. It wrote 17,000 lines of C++ and reproduced 36 percent of the program's behavior. The code was solid and the common paths worked, but most of the program was still missing. It did not run out of time or budget. It stopped because, by its own assessment, it was done.
We then arranged Droid into a system consisting of separate roles. Before any implementation, one role built an executable standard of completion - its own account of what the reimplementation must do and what evidence would prove it - and the implementation was then held to that standard. This run grew to 115,000 lines and reached 90 percent behavioral parity.
What the system run produced is 
its own program
: it resembles the original in neither shape nor size - a fraction of GDAL's codebase, organized its own way.
This was not an outlier case. Across the 24 tasks, the same system took its 7-Zip recreation from 54 percent parity to 95 percent and its DuckDB recreation from 34 to 80 percent. Several recreations reached the upper 90s.
The underlying model did not change. But when held to its own standard of completion, it reproduced far more of each program's behavior.


[H3 id] why-the-same-agent-stops-early


#### Why the same agent stops early
Coding agents usually validate their own work as they go. They implement a piece, write or run a few checks, inspect the output, and decide whether to continue. For a small change, this works well: the task, implementation, and evidence fit in one view.
Large tasks have to be decomposed into features, subsystems, and successive rounds of work. As the agent reaches each piece, it also decides what evidence would count and whether that evidence is sufficient. These checks inherit the scope of the work that produced them. They can establish everything the agent thought to build, but exclude features, interactions, or constraints it never represented.
An agent can therefore make steady, locally correct progress and stop with much of the outcome absent. The problem is not necessarily that it could not implement the rest. It never established a complete account of what remained.


[H3 id] define-validation-before-the-work


#### Define validation before the work
Establishing a whole outcome requires more than a list of requirements. The system needs an inventory of what must be established, procedures for establishing each part, and current evidence that those procedures pass against the artifact being shipped.
That standard should be derived from the requirements and relevant sources of truth before implementation narrows the task into individual work items. It need not remain frozen. Checks can be added, replaced, or refined as the system learns. But the standard of completion must not quietly collapse around whatever has already been built.


[H3 id] why-this-is-rarely-done-by-humans


#### Why this is rarely done by humans
Separating requirements from evidence is not new. Safety-critical projects use requirements traceability and independent verification and validation. Standards bodies publish conformance suites that many implementations must pass. Product teams write acceptance tests.
What is unusual is deriving and maintaining a comprehensive standard for each project. A conformance suite can spread its cost across many implementations; a product team bears that cost again for each application, rewrite, or migration. Most teams therefore validate incrementally and rely on review, product feedback, and the continuity of the people involved to preserve the whole.
Agents change both sides of this tradeoff. They can produce work faster than humans can inspect it, making informal supervision the bottleneck. But the same capacity can be applied to the standard itself: inventorying the outcome, constructing checks, and rerunning them as the artifact changes.
ProgramBench represents a demanding limit case: the reference program is available, but the model must discover both the behavior space and how to measure it.


[H3 id] programbench


#### ProgramBench
ProgramBench is a cleanroom software-engineering benchmark. Each task provides a reference program, fixtures, and partial documentation. The reference is a black-box oracle: it may be run, but never read, decompiled, or traced.

content.content:
ProgramBench is a cleanroom software-engineering benchmark. Each task provides a reference program, fixtures, and partial documentation. The reference is a black-box oracle: it may be run, but never read, decompiled, or traced.
The goal is to reproduce the observable behavior of the reference program from scratch. Each task is graded and scored against a hidden suite of behavioral checks.
Completeness of a black-box implementation is difficult to measure. Any single behavior is trivially verifiable by running the reference against the candidate, but the whole is not. The shipped documentation covers a slice of the interface; the rest of the program's behavior has to be discovered.
That leaves three questions:
Can a frontier model construct its own measure of completeness for a large, unknown program?
Can that measure remain useful through a long implementation?
Does answering to it produce a better artifact?


[H3 id] task-selection


#### Task selection
We selected 24 of the benchmark's hardest tasks, based on the current top leaderboard score.
The set was hand-picked, weighted toward low best-public scores. Some hard-end candidates (php-src, pueue, ditaa, quickjs, chroma, miller) were dropped during screening for persistent safety blocks, single-agent saturation, or a score gated by one undocumented environment variable.


[H3 id] experimental-design


#### Experimental design
For each selected task and model panel, we ran one campaign in each of two conditions. The system condition added an independent measure of completion without replacing the implementer's ordinary development loop.
Single-agent campaign
System campaign
Implementation loop
Agent investigates, implements, runs checks, and judges its work
Implementer investigates, implements, runs checks, and judges its work
Completion standard
Develops inside the same context as the candidate
Validator constructs an independent instrument before implementation
Independent measurement
None during the campaign
Validator measures successive candidates against its instrument
Information flow
Agent sees all checks and results
Instrument and raw results remain with the validator; clustered findings cross the wall
Campaign control
Agent chooses what to do next and when to stop
Orchestrator adjudicates findings, issues directives, and decides when to ship
Both conditions began from the same task scaffold and fixtures. Within each non-substituted model panel, the single agent and all three system roles used the same model at the same reasoning level. Both conditions could execute the reference program without limit, but neither could read, decompile, or trace it, inspect the benchmark tests, or access the internet. Six disclosed Fable cells used Opus after Fable was safety-blocked.
Once launched, each campaign ran without human intervention. The campaigns were not compute-matched; each continued until the single agent or system orchestrator decided to ship.
Each cell represents one campaign, not an average across repeated runs. After a campaign ended, its final candidate was graded once using the official pb-1.2.0 metric.


[H3 id] how-the-system-closed-the-loop


#### How the system closed the loop


[H4 id] the-instrument


#### The instrument
Full behavioral parity is not directly measurable. A program can accept an effectively unbounded set of inputs, flags, file formats, combinations, and error conditions. Any practical validation strategy has to sample that space.
In our system, that sample is an instrument. Before implementation begins, a validator surveys the reference program and maps where its behavior lives. It then builds a weighted body of cases and the comparison rules needed to judge the candidate's output. We asked for the instrument only in outline. Everything inside it - which behaviors matter, how they are weighted, what counts as evidence - the validator decides.
Two cases from the instrument the validator built for 
gdal
D('hillshade.combined', ['raster', 'hillshade', '--variant', 'combined', 'dem.tif', 'out.tif']),
D('contour.levels', ['raster', 'contour', '--levels', '120,150,180', 'dem.tif', 'out.geojson']),
Each case describes the invocation; the grading policy says how to judge the result:
Primary comparator: for every case, the runner executes oracle and candidate sequentially in the same absolute sandbox path (wiped between runs), same env, same fixture bytes and mtimes, and byte-compares four channels:

1. exit code
2. stdout bytes
3. stderr bytes
4. full work-tree delta: the set of files created/modified/deleted by the run, and the exact bytes of each (includes sidecars: .aux.xml, .ovr, .msk, shapefile companions, tile trees).

Byte identity is the default on every channel. A relaxation exists only as a named normalizer attached to specific cases, each carrying a license below.
The validator wrote hundreds of cases like these, and licensed exactly two relaxations across all of them - a masked heap address in debug traces, a date embedded in a file header - each with recorded evidence that the reference cannot produce stable bytes there.


[H4 id] the-outer-loop


#### The outer loop
The system consists of three roles: orchestrator, implementer, and validator. The orchestrator delegates to both the implementer, which builds the candidate program, and the validator, which measures it against its instrument.
The validator builds the instrument first. Once implementation starts, the loop goes:
The orchestrator chooses what should be measured.
The validator tests the current candidate and interprets the failures.
The orchestrator decides which findings are real and what work should happen next.
The implementer investigates the reference and advances the candidate.
When the instrument stops revealing meaningful differences between successive candidates, the orchestrator can ask the validator to expand a weak area or begin targeted differential testing against the reference.


[H4 id] the-wall


#### The wall
In ProgramBench, the standard required an additional boundary because its cases were only a sample of a much larger behavior space.
The boundary holds in both directions. The validator can expand the instrument as it learns more about the reference, but cannot weaken or revise it to accommodate what the candidate happens to contain. And the implementer never authors it, runs it, or sees its cases or raw output: once a sparse sample becomes visible, it becomes the target, and passing it establishes those cases, not the space they were meant to represent.
The validator runs the instrument against the current candidate and groups failures by root cause. The orchestrator reviews those findings, rejects noise or invalid measurements, and turns the remaining problems into a directive at the level of missing features, subsystems, or behavior. The implementer receives the directive, investigates the reference independently, and decides how to change the candidate.

gdal

The directive tells the implementer where the candidate is weak without giving away the sample.


[H3 id] results


#### Results
We ran the experiment with three frontier models - Fable 5, Kimi K3, and GPT 5.6 Sol.
Every score here comes from the benchmark's hidden suite - a sample of the same behavior space that no role ever saw. The gains transferred from the instrument the system built to an independent measure.
Each panel is one model, run twice on the same 24 tasks: on the left as a
single agent, on the right as the full system. Every line is one task,
placed at its official score from the benchmark's hidden suite. Lines that
fall are drawn dashed. A handful of cells have no score at all, a test
hung during evaluation, so grading never completed. These are placed at
the foot of the panel. The rail on the left filters the tasks by
difficulty, the best public score per task, on the same 0-100 scale.
The system runs were far longer and more expensive; for 
gdal
, 14 times the credits and 13 times the wall time. But budget was not what separated the conditions. Every single-agent campaign ended because the agent decided to end it. Additional compute does not help an agent that will not spend it. What our approach changed was the judgment of completion; the compute followed from that judgment.

[H4 id] every-task-every-model


#### Every task, every model


[H4 id] method-notes


#### Method notes
Reasoning levels.
 Fable ran at xhigh, Kimi at high, Sol at max, applied uniformly to the single agent and to all three roles in the system.
One run per cell.
 Every number here is a single run. Nothing was repeated to average it, so no cell carries a variance estimate, and none of these figures should be read as a mean.
Headline runs.
 The gdal, 7-Zip, and DuckDB numbers in the opening section are Fable 5 runs.
Scale.
 GDAL upstream is roughly two million lines of C/C++ (1.9 million after removing bundled third-party libraries). The subset reachable through the 
gdal
 CLI as configured in the task - eleven drivers, no GEOS - is roughly 600 thousand. The recreation matched 90 percent of that surface's measured behavior in 115 thousand lines.
Opus substitutes.
 Six cells in the Fable panel are Opus runs standing in for Fable ones that were safety-blocked, either in the single-agent or system run: bedtools2, gromacs, pandoc, samtools, sox and tree-sitter.
Coverage.
 141 of the 144 cells have been graded. The remaining three system runs - gdal and gromacs on Sol, samtools on Kimi - were interrupted and not rerun before publication; they carry no score.
Grading.
 Every score is the official metric from the hidden suite, pinned at pb-1.2.0 and computed identically for single-agent and system artifacts.


[H3 id] conclusion


#### Conclusion
The single agent didn't lack skill. It lacked a standard of completion. An independent standard, authored by the same model, drove the implementation much closer to behavioral parity with the reference.
ProgramBench gave that standard a particular shape: an inventory and weighted sample recovered from a black-box reference.
Other tasks draw their standard from different sources. A product task may draw on user-approved flows and designs; a migration, on the system being replaced.
What generalizes to real software work is the need for an external, executable standard of completion - one derived from the outcome, before implementation narrows attention, and kept current until the work meets it.
We are building this structure into the next generation of Missions.
